extracted.intended_audience: aspiring op-ed/commentary writers pitching opinion pieces to newspapers, magazines, and online outlets (including under-represented experts)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for crafting and pitching short-form opinion pieces (op-eds) that are timely, evidence-based, and persuasive to general-news and specialty outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what you are an expert in and why - but don’t limit yourself. Consider the metaphors that your experience and knowledge suggest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about why you are qualified to write on the topic. Use personal experience and professional perspective as affordances for argument. (The OpEd Project recommends workshops to help hone this.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay current
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the news – both general and specific to your areas of specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the relevant press for the topic you write about (e.g., read the Haitian press if writing about Haiti). Staying current helps you find timely news hooks and connect your knowledge to current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: The perfect is the enemy of the good (write fast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write fast. You may have only a few hours to get your piece in before the moment is gone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize speed when an op-ed is pegged to a short-lived news hook. Draft quickly and be prepared to move on if an editor passes; you can re-pitch elsewhere later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a flexible mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A good idea may have more than one news hook; keep an eye out for surprising connections and new news hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to reframe your piece around different timely angles. If one outlet passes, another news hook or angle may make it publishable later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon serves a purpose, but it is rarely useful in public debate. Speak to your reader in straight talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid technical language that obscures your argument. Make complex ideas accessible without dumbing them down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect your reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Never underestimate your reader’s intelligence, or overestimate her level of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume a non-expert audience and provide necessary context succinctly. Capture attention and make the argument compelling without lecturing or condescension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish credibility: Why should readers trust you?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you authoritative on your topic? Are you accountable to what you say you know? Can you provide evidence of your expertise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don’t need celebrity or high-status credentials, but you must show you are well positioned to speak on the topic (e.g., first-hand experience, relevant role, documented work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up claims with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Is your argument based on evidence – solid material and logical building blocks that will be acknowledged as credible even by those who may disagree?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics, reputable studies, reports, expert quotes, history, and first‑hand experience. Avoid unsupported assertions; ensure sources are credible to skeptical readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: What's new? (original contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is your argument different, particularly original in the way it is delivered, or is it backed up by substantially new information or reporting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An op-ed should offer a fresh angle, original framing, or new facts that justify publication. If the idea isn’t novel, emphasize a distinctive delivery or new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: So what? (relevance and urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should everyone else – including non-experts – care?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the broader stakes of your argument explicit: policy implications, practical consequences, or moral urgency. Tie specifics to larger public concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be effective, not just right (tone and persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does your language tend to write off people who would disagree with you, or do you employ empathy and respect to change minds?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid alienating rhetoric. Use empathetic framing and respect to persuade rather than simply assert correctness. Distinguish between being factually right and being rhetorically effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and usefulness of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: How will your ideas and arguments contribute to the conversation, and be helpful to your audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present practical implications, solutions, or clarifications that readers (and editors) will find useful. Think in terms of contribution, not just critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: Lede with a news hook
rubrics_metrics.description: A lede sets the scene and grabs attention; a news hook makes your piece timely and is often part of the lede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be bold but incontrovertible. Use an anecdote, news event, study, anniversary, or cultural reference as an entry point. The lede should orient readers quickly to why the piece matters now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: Make a clear argument supported by points and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: State your argument (explicit or implied), then make 1–3 supporting points each backed by evidence (stats, reports, quotes, history, first-hand experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common structure: Lede/news hook → thesis/argument → 1st point + evidence → conclusion for that point → 2nd point + evidence → 3rd point + evidence (or broader context) → conclusion. Keep each point tightly tied to the central thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a 'To Be Sure' paragraph to pre-empt critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-empt potential critics by acknowledging flaws and addressing obvious counter-arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concede limited points where appropriate, then explain why your overall argument still holds. This increases credibility and diffuses predictable rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion should often circle back to the lede
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion typically returns to the opening and reinforces the central point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with a memorable line, a call to action, or a restatement of significance that connects back to the lede and leaves the reader with a clear takeaway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede/news-hook techniques and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Ways to open: use breaking news, tell a dramatic anecdote, reference popular culture, turn conventional wisdom on its head, use wit/irony, mark an anniversary, cite a major new study, or get personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides multiple exemplar openings (e.g., executions, Bosnian anecdote, marketing campaign ad, Sex and the City reversal, anniversary of Brown v. Board, citing a nationwide poll, personal admissions). Use samples as models for tone and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate outlets and research target publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets vary in flavor and selectivity; research and understand the target publisher before submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim high but have backup outlets (plan B, C, D). Smaller or niche outlets may offer better odds and help build a track record toward larger publications. Tailor submissions to each outlet's readership and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and follow-up etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: When to check in with an editor depends on the shelf life of your idea; give more time for evergreen pieces and move quickly for short-lived hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For time-sensitive pieces, follow up within 24–48 hours; for evergreen items, wait a week or more. Be polite, not demanding; assume silence often means a pass and re-submit elsewhere if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous submissions policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most national newspapers will not consider your piece if you submit to more than one paper at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each outlet’s policy before simultaneous submission. If you do submit simultaneously, be aware that many top outlets expect exclusive consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch and submission support (use resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek pitching help via workshops, mentor-editors, and live 'Ask A Journalist' office hours where editors may live-edit drafts and pitches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available institutional supports (e.g., OpEd Project workshops and mentor network) for feedback on drafts and pitches; live editing can substantially improve odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of submissions and editorial tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: You may submit as often as you want, but many outlets won't publish the same author frequently; submissions should be pegged to timely hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeatedly sending similar off-base ideas to the same editors; listen to feedback (including silence) as signals about fit. Cultivate relationships with editors who respond positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rejection constructively
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat rejection as information, not failure; seek feedback and iterate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an editor provides reasons, thank them and ask what would have made the piece more valuable. Use rejections to refine ideas and develop future pitches; persistence and learning can lead to eventual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of representation and data on submission demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors note large disparities in submission and byline gender ratios; awareness may motivate outreach and tracking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that some outlets have historically seen far more submissions and bylines from men; the page suggests outlets could survey submitter demographics to better reach under-represented voices.
